chapters.n: The story opens in the unsettled era of the judges, when Israel often strayed and suffered. A famine pushes one Bethlehem family to move east across the Jordan to Moab, a neighboring nation often hostile to Israel.

f.g: Bethlehem (“house of bread”) in Judah, distinguishing it from a Bethlehem in Zebulun. Later the birthplace of David and of Jesus.

chapters.n: The family members are named. Their names carry meaning: Elimelech means “my God is king” and Naomi means “pleasant,” which becomes important when Naomi later asks to be renamed.

f.g: Ephrath or Ephratah was an older name for the Bethlehem area.

chapters.n: Tragedy strikes: Naomi's husband dies in a foreign land, leaving her a widow far from home with only her two sons to support her.
Naomi's sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. The family stays in Moab about ten years, putting down roots outside the covenant land.
Both sons die as well, so Naomi is left with no husband and no sons. In that world, this meant no income, no protection, and no one to carry on the family name.

f.g: Widows without sons were among the most vulnerable people in ancient society; the law repeatedly commands care for them.

chapters.n: Naomi hears that the famine back home has ended. The text credits the Lord with sending food again, a quiet reminder that God is at work behind the scenes of this whole story.

f.g: To “visit” here means to come to someone's aid with care and blessing.

chapters.n: Naomi sets out for Judah, and both daughters-in-law begin the journey with her, showing their affection for her.
On the road Naomi urges the young women to go back to their own mothers' homes. She blesses them, praying the Lord will show them the same kindness they have shown her family.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — loyal, covenant love; faithful kindness that goes beyond duty. It is the key word of the book of Ruth.

chapters.n: Naomi hopes they will each find “rest” — the security of a new home and husband. The farewell is tearful because they truly love one another.

f.g: Here, settled security and safety in a household.

chapters.n: At first both women insist on staying with Naomi and going to her people.
Naomi reasons with them: she has no more sons to give them as husbands. She is thinking of the custom where a brother would marry his dead brother's widow to keep the family line alive.

f.w: that they may be your husbands
f.g: A reference to levirate marriage, where a brother-in-law married a childless widow.

chapters.n: Naomi presses her point: she is too old to remarry, and even if she married that very night and had sons, the timing would be impossible.

f.g: Go back; return home.

chapters.n: Would they wait decades for babies to grow up? Naomi feels her losses as the Lord's hand against her, and she does not want the young women to share her hardship.

f.g: wait

chapters.n: After more tears, Orpah kisses Naomi goodbye and turns back, a sensible choice. But Ruth holds tight to Naomi and will not let go.

f.g: clung, held fast. The same word describes a husband cleaving to his wife.

chapters.n: Naomi points out that Orpah has returned to her people and her gods, and urges Ruth to do the same. Choosing Naomi would mean leaving Moab's religion behind.

f.g: Moab's chief god was Chemosh.

chapters.n: Ruth answers with one of scripture's most beautiful vows of loyalty. She binds herself not just to Naomi but to Israel and to Israel's God — a true conversion.
Ruth's commitment is for life and beyond: she will even be buried in Naomi's land. She seals it with a solemn oath in the name of the LORD, Israel's God.

f.w: the LORD do so to me, and more also
f.g: A standard oath formula: may God punish me severely if I break this promise.

chapters.n: Seeing that Ruth's mind is firmly made up, Naomi stops arguing.

f.g: firmly determined

chapters.n: The two women reach Bethlehem, and the whole town buzzes. The women of the town can hardly recognize Naomi after ten hard years.

f.g: stirred up, excited

chapters.n: Naomi asks to be called Mara (“bitter”) instead of Naomi (“pleasant”). Her grief is honest; scripture allows her to voice her pain to and about God.

f.g: Hebrew for “bitter.”
Hebrew Shaddai, an ancient title for God.

chapters.n: She left with a husband and sons and returns with nothing — or so she thinks. Readers notice the irony: she has come home with Ruth, who will become her greatest blessing.

f.g: Naomi feels as if God has brought a case against her.

chapters.n: The chapter closes with hope: they arrive just as barley harvest begins in spring, setting the stage for Ruth's gleaning and for the Lord's provision.

f.g: Barley ripened first, around April, followed by wheat a few weeks later.

chapters.n: The narrator introduces Boaz before Ruth meets him: a relative of Elimelech and a man of wealth and standing. The reader now knows something Ruth does not.

f.g: A relative in the clan who could have duties to help family in need.
The Hebrew can mean wealthy, capable, or of strong character — Boaz is all three.

chapters.n: Ruth takes the initiative to support Naomi by gleaning, hoping to find a landowner who will be kind to a foreigner. Naomi gives her blessing.

f.g: To gather leftover grain the harvesters missed. God's law required farmers to leave these for the poor, foreigners, widows, and orphans.
In KJV English, “corn” means grain in general — here, barley.

chapters.n: Ruth “happens” to land in the field of Boaz. The narrator's understatement invites readers to see God's quiet guidance in what looks like chance.

f.w: her hap was to light on
f.g: As it happened, she came upon — a gentle hint of providence.

chapters.n: Boaz greets his workers in the Lord's name and they bless him in return. This small exchange shows a godly, respectful workplace.
Boaz notices the stranger among the gleaners and asks his foreman who she belongs to — that is, whose family she is part of.

f.g: young woman

chapters.n: The foreman identifies her by her foreign origin: the Moabite woman who returned with Naomi. Word of Ruth had already spread in the small town.
The foreman reports that Ruth asked permission politely and has worked hard since morning with only a short rest. Her diligence matches her loyalty.

f.g: stayed, rested

chapters.n: Boaz speaks to Ruth tenderly, calling her “my daughter” (he is likely older). He invites her to stay in his field with his young women, where she will be safe.

f.g: stay close beside

chapters.n: Boaz protects Ruth from harassment by ordering the young men not to bother her, and gives her access to the water the workers drew — generous treatment for a gleaner.

f.g: thirsty
Here, to bother, harm, or harass.

chapters.n: Ruth bows to the ground in deep gratitude, amazed that he would notice and care for a foreigner like her.

f.g: notice me, pay attention to me. In Hebrew this sounds like the word for “foreigner,” a wordplay.
foreigner, outsider

chapters.n: Boaz explains that he has heard all about her kindness to Naomi and her courage in leaving her homeland. Like Abraham, she left family and country to come to a land she did not know.

f.w: left thy father and thy mother, and the land of thy nativity

chapters.n: Boaz prays that the Lord will reward Ruth. He pictures her as a young bird sheltering under God's wings — a lovely image of trust and protection.

f.g: repay, reward

chapters.n: Ruth humbly thanks Boaz for comforting her and speaking kindly, even though she does not have the standing of one of his own servant girls.

f.g: Literally “spoken to the heart” — spoken kindly and reassuringly.

chapters.n: Boaz invites Ruth to eat with the workers and personally serves her roasted grain. She eats until satisfied and still has food left over to take home to Naomi.

f.g: Probably a sour wine or vinegar dip used to flavor bread.
roasted grain
satisfied, full

chapters.n: Boaz goes beyond the law's requirement, letting Ruth glean even among the bundled sheaves, normally off-limits, and telling his men not to shame her.

f.g: do not embarrass or scold her

chapters.n: He even has the workers drop extra grain on purpose for her. Generosity done quietly, without humiliating the receiver, reflects the Lord's own kindness.

f.g: on purpose, deliberately

chapters.n: Ruth works until evening and threshes her grain: about an ephah of barley, a remarkably large amount for one day of gleaning.

f.g: A dry measure of roughly 20–40 pounds of grain — perhaps weeks of food for two women.
threshed — beat the stalks to separate the grain

chapters.n: Ruth carries the grain home and also gives Naomi the leftover roasted grain from lunch. Naomi's emptiness is beginning to be filled.
Naomi is astonished at the amount and blesses whoever helped Ruth. Only at the end does Ruth reveal the man's name — Boaz — a dramatic moment in the story.

f.g: did you work

chapters.n: Naomi's bitterness softens to praise: the Lord has not stopped showing kindness to the living (Naomi and Ruth) and the dead (their husbands). She reveals Boaz is a close relative with family duties.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — loyal covenant love.
Hebrew go'el — a kinsman-redeemer who could buy back family land, free relatives from debt, or marry a widow to preserve the family name.

chapters.n: Ruth adds that Boaz invited her to stay with his workers through the whole harvest. Her continued title “the Moabitess” reminds us she is still an outsider being welcomed in.
Naomi agrees this is wise, since in another field Ruth might be mistreated. Naomi is now actively looking out for Ruth's welfare.

f.g: The sense is “so that no one harms you.”

chapters.n: Ruth gleans with Boaz's workers through both the barley and wheat harvests — about seven weeks — while living with and caring for Naomi.

f.g: Wheat harvest ended around the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost), about seven weeks after barley harvest began.

chapters.n: Now Naomi takes the initiative. Just as Ruth cared for her, she wants to secure “rest” for Ruth — a safe, settled home through marriage.
Naomi reminds Ruth that Boaz is a relative and tells her he will be at the threshing floor that night, winnowing barley.

f.g: Tosses threshed grain into the evening breeze so the wind blows away the light chaff while the heavier grain falls.
A flat, hard area outside town where grain was processed; owners often slept there at harvest to guard the grain.

chapters.n: Naomi tells Ruth to bathe, perfume herself, and put on her best clothing — perhaps signaling the end of her mourning — and to wait until Boaz has finished his meal.

f.g: Put on scented oil.
clothing

chapters.n: Ruth is to uncover Boaz's feet and lie down there. This was a bold but proper way to make a request; Boaz would then decide what to do.

f.g: A symbolic act asking for his protection and attention; the story treats it as honorable, not immoral (see verse 11).

chapters.n: Ruth trusts Naomi completely and agrees to follow her plan.
Ruth goes to the threshing floor and carries out Naomi's instructions exactly.
After a satisfying harvest meal, Boaz settles down to sleep beside the grain pile. Ruth quietly uncovers his feet and lies down.

f.g: He was content and in good spirits after a good harvest and meal.

chapters.n: At midnight Boaz wakes with a start — perhaps from the chill on his feet — and discovers a woman lying at his feet.

f.g: was startled

chapters.n: Ruth identifies herself and boldly asks Boaz to spread his garment over her — a request for marriage — because he is a kinsman-redeemer with the right to help the family.

f.g: “Skirt” is the corner of a garment; the same Hebrew word is “wings.” Ruth asks Boaz to be the answer to his own prayer about God's wings.
Hebrew go'el, kinsman-redeemer.

chapters.n: Boaz blesses Ruth for this second act of loyal love. She could have pursued a younger man, but chose to marry within Naomi's family to preserve its name.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — loyal covenant love.

chapters.n: Boaz reassures Ruth and promises to do what she asks. The whole town knows she is a woman of noble character.

f.g: Hebrew ’eshet ḥayil, “a woman of strength/worth” — the same phrase as Proverbs 31, and matching the description of Boaz in Ruth 2:1.

chapters.n: But there is a complication: another relative is more closely related and has the first right to act as redeemer.
Boaz promises with an oath that if the nearer relative will not redeem, he will. He asks Ruth to rest until morning, protecting her from traveling home in the dark.

f.g: To act as go'el — redeem the land and marry the widow to raise up the family name.
A solemn oath.

chapters.n: Ruth leaves before dawn, while it is too dark to recognize anyone. Boaz wants to protect her reputation from gossip.

f.g: before it was light enough to recognize faces

chapters.n: Boaz fills Ruth's shawl with a generous amount of barley as a gift — a sign of his good faith and a promise of more to come.

f.g: Probably a large shawl or cloak.
The unit is not stated; it was as much as Ruth could carry.

chapters.n: Naomi eagerly asks how things went, and Ruth tells her everything Boaz did.

f.g: Probably means “How did it go?” or “What is your situation now?”

chapters.n: Ruth reports Boaz's words: he did not want her to return to Naomi empty-handed. This answers Naomi's earlier lament that she came home “empty.”
Naomi tells Ruth to wait patiently; Boaz is a man of his word and will settle the matter that very day.

f.g: wait patiently

chapters.n: Boaz goes straight to the city gate, the town's public square and courtroom. The nearer relative happens by, and Boaz calls him over. The narrator leaves him unnamed — he never earns a lasting name.

f.g: The gate area was where business, legal cases, and public agreements were settled before witnesses.
Hebrew peloni almoni, roughly “so-and-so” — the narrator withholds his name.

chapters.n: Boaz gathers ten elders as official witnesses, making this a legally binding public proceeding.
Boaz raises the matter: Naomi must sell (or transfer the rights to) the land that belonged to Elimelech, and a relative has the right to keep it in the family.

f.g: “Brother” here means relative or clansman.

chapters.n: Boaz formally offers the nearer kinsman first right to redeem the land, with himself next in line. Gaining extra land seems attractive, so the man agrees.

f.g: inform you, let you know
To buy back property or people so they stay within the family; the same idea is used for the Lord's redeeming of His people.

chapters.n: Then Boaz reveals the catch: whoever takes the land also takes responsibility for Ruth, marrying her so that a son can carry on the dead husband's name and inherit the land.

f.w: raise up the name of the dead

chapters.n: The relative backs out. A son born to Ruth would inherit the land, so his investment would not benefit his own estate. He gives his right to Boaz.

f.g: damage or endanger my own estate

chapters.n: The narrator explains an old custom: to seal a transfer of rights, a man removed his sandal and gave it to the other party, like signing a contract.

f.g: A sandal may have symbolized the right to walk on and possess land.
exchanging or transferring property

chapters.n: The relative tells Boaz to buy it himself and hands over his sandal, completing the legal transfer.
Boaz publicly declares that he has acquired all the property of Elimelech and his sons from Naomi, and calls the crowd to witness.
Boaz also declares that he takes Ruth as his wife to preserve Mahlon's name and inheritance. His willingness to give, rather than gain, shows true redemption.

f.g: acquired; here a legal term for taking on the marriage responsibility, not buying a slave.
not forgotten or erased from the family records

chapters.n: The witnesses bless the marriage, praying Ruth will be like Rachel and Leah, the mothers of Israel's tribes, and that Boaz will prosper and be honored.

f.g: Bethlehem's ancient clan name.

chapters.n: They also wish Boaz's family to be like that of Pharez, Judah's son by Tamar — another story in which an outsider woman preserved a family line, and Boaz's own ancestor.

f.w: Pharez, whom Tamar bare unto Judah

chapters.n: Boaz marries Ruth, and the Lord grants her a son. The text credits God with the gift of conception, the quiet hand of God showing again.
The women of Bethlehem praise the Lord for giving Naomi a redeemer. The empty woman of chapter 1 is now full.

f.g: Here the go'el is the baby boy, who will carry on the family name.

chapters.n: This grandson will renew Naomi's life and care for her in old age. And the women honor Ruth: her love is worth more than seven sons — the ideal number of a perfect family.

f.g: Literally, “one who brings back your soul” — the same verb as Naomi's “returning” in chapter 1.

chapters.n: Naomi holds the baby close and helps raise him. The woman who lost everything now cradles new life.

f.g: Here, a caregiver or guardian, not a wet nurse.

chapters.n: The neighbors name the child Obed, and the narrator reveals the surprise: he is grandfather of King David. A Moabite convert's faithfulness leads to Israel's royal line.

f.g: Means “servant” or “worshipper.”

chapters.n: A closing genealogy traces the family from Pharez, son of Judah, forward. Genealogies in scripture show how God's promises unfold across generations.
The line continues through Hezron and Ram to Amminadab, whose daughter married Aaron.
Nahshon was leader of the tribe of Judah during the wilderness journey with Moses. Salmon is listed in Matthew as married to Rahab of Jericho.
Salmon is the father of Boaz, and Boaz the father of Obed. If Matthew's record is followed, both Boaz's mother (Rahab) and his wife (Ruth) were converts from outside Israel.
The book ends with David, Israel's great king. Through David's line would come Jesus Christ, the ultimate Redeemer, born in this same town of Bethlehem.
